$comment: THE MACHINE-CHECKED SCOPE OF THE 2.0 BASELINE.
Phase 9 as specified creates "every cross-domain table in §3". §3 names ~180 tenant
tables and gives a full CREATE TABLE for twelve of them, two of which §6 assigns to
other phases. So the baseline inherits ten specified tables and fifty-odd that exist
only as a name in a list — eighteen of which appear exactly once in the whole 900-line
document. Inventing their columns in a SQUASHED BASELINE is the expensive direction:
a later migration that adds a table is cheap, and a wrong column type is a data
So this file names every table §3 mentions and what was done about it. It is not
documentation: `pnpm check:schema-conventions` fails if a v2 model has no entry here,
and `tenant-schema-census.spec.ts` fails if a `created` table is missing from a freshly
provisioned database or if a `deferred` one has appeared. "We did not build these" is
therefore a fact CI enforces, not an omission a reviewer has to notice.
Names were extracted mechanically from the `·`-separated inventory paragraphs of §3.
The `phase` on a deferred entry is the owning MILESTONE from §6, not a per-table claim.

calendar_exception_hours.reason: NOT A §3 TABLE. §3's Circulation line names `calendars`, `calendar_hours` and `calendar_exceptions` and stops, which leaves "we open late on 24 December" nowhere to live — an exception can only close a day, never re-open it on different hours. The alternative to a second table was a nullable `date` on `calendar_hours` beside its nullable `weekday`: a CHECK that exactly one is set, two partial indexes, and one relation read with two meanings. This costs one more join in a query that runs once per snapshot build and makes the wrong shape unrepresentable instead of merely constrained. Absence is again the encoding — an exception row with no children is a CLOSURE — and non-empty hours REPLACE the weekday's rather than merging with them, because "we are shut on 25 December" and "we open late on the 24th" are the same kind of statement and a merge cannot express the first. It carries its own no-overlap `EXCLUDE USING gist` for the reason `calendar_hours` does.

calendar_exceptions.reason: §3 names it once with no DDL. ONE CIVIL DATE, NOT A RANGE: a three-week August closure is 21 rows. That is the shape `CalendarException` has in `types.ts`, and it is what keeps `hoursOn(calendar, date)` a keyed lookup on a path that walks up to `ROLL_HORIZON_DAYS` = 45 candidate days per due date. It also makes uniqueness a plain unique index (`calendar_exceptions_one_per_date`) rather than an `EXCLUDE`: two exceptions on ONE date collide exactly, and `23505` says so at a fraction of the cost. `name` is stored because the resolution trace has to be able to answer "why is this due on the 19th?" with «Δεκαπενταύγουστος» rather than "a closed day", and `source` separates the seeder's regenerable `greek_public_holiday` rows from a librarian's own, which are never touched.

calendar_hours.reason: §3 names it once with no DDL. ONE ROW PER INTERVAL, not per weekday, and that is the whole reason this is a table rather than two columns on `calendars`: the Greek split day (διακεκομμένο ωράριο) — 08:00–14:00 then 17:00–21:00 — is the ordinary shape of a municipal library here, and an open/close pair per weekday cannot hold it. `isOpenAt(14:30)` would answer open while the desk is shut, and "end of the open day" would come out 14:00 rather than 21:00. Minutes from local midnight rather than `time`, so every comparison in `circ-policy` is integer arithmetic — measured 415× cheaper than the `Intl` round trip it replaces — and so `close_min` can exceed 1440 for a desk that shuts after midnight, which `time` cannot express at all. A weekday with no rows is CLOSED all day; absence is the encoding, which is why there is no `closed boolean`. Overlapping intervals are refused by an `EXCLUDE USING gist`, because `hoursOn` returns stored order and `isOpenAt` takes the first interval containing the minute, so 08:00–14:00 overlapping 13:00–21:00 gives an "open until" that depends on row order.

calendars.reason: §3 names it in one inventory line and gives no DDL, so every column is designed and the design is "whatever `packages/circ-policy/src/types.ts` needs, and nothing else" — phase 12 fixed that vocabulary against 630 golden vectors before there was a column to hold it. Two decisions are not obvious from the model. `defined_from`/`defined_to` are `date`, not `timestamptz(3)`: "the calendar is defined through 31 December 2028" is true in every zone, and storing it as an instant makes it true at 02:00 in one and 23:00 in another. And the range is BOUNDED on purpose — a resolver asked about a date past it raises `calendarNotDefinedFor` rather than assuming "open, normal hours", because assuming is how a library fines a patron for a day it was shut. There is deliberately NO timezone column: the zone is `branches.timezone`, a second copy is a second answer to "what zone is this library in?", and the copy that is wrong is the one nobody edits. This also gives `branches.calendar_id` the foreign key §3 left undecided, `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, because a branch whose calendar was deleted cannot compute a due date at all. Phase 23 owns the UI that fills these in.

cancellation_reasons.reason: Re-phased by 17, which owns `holds` and deliberately did NOT create it. `holds.cancelled_reason` is free text, because what phase 17 owes is that a job-written cancellation is READABLE, and a sentence is. Phase 21 already owns `override_reasons`, which is the same shape of librarian-configurable vocabulary table, and phase 15 sent the three item condition codes there for the same reason: the machinery should be built once, by the phase that has two callers for it.

circulation_policy_version.reason: §3 names it once in the Circulation line and gives no DDL; §4.1 supplies the design in one phrase — the snapshot is "versioned by the trigger-maintained `circulation_policy_version` counter". Trigger-maintained is the whole point, and the argument is sharper than the changelog's: a forgotten `emit()` breaks a replica, but a forgotten BUMP means every pod keeps its cached snapshot, the 30-second backstop re-reads the counter, sees no change and keeps the stale cache — not for thirty seconds but FOREVER. The librarian edits the loan period, the screen says saved, and every checkout that week uses the old one. Fourteen `AFTER … FOR EACH STATEMENT` triggers cover all six writers: this phase's service, the simple-mode façade, a phase-30 importer, phase 19's PL/pgSQL copy-forward, a seed script, and a support engineer in `psql`. `integer`, not `bigint` and not a timestamp: Prisma maps `BigInt` to a JS `bigint` and `JSON.stringify({version: 1n})` THROWS, and this number lands in `loans.policy_snapshot jsonb` on every checkout, while `now()` is TRANSACTION START time, so a long transaction that commits second stamps first and a "rebuild if stored > cached" cache never rebuilds again. The INTEGER `id` is allowed by rule 4 only alongside an unquoted `ALTER TABLE circulation_policy_version … CHECK (id = 1)`, written by hand because Prisma quotes and the gate's regex does not match a quoted table name.

circulation_rules.reason: §3 gives it a full CREATE TABLE and every clause of it is here, including both partial unique indexes, hand-written because Prisma cannot express them. TWO DEPARTURES, both deliberate. `specificity` is a GENERATED STORED column, which Prisma has no concept of, so it is absent from the datamodel and the drop `migrate diff` proposes on every run is allowlisted in `scripts/check-schema-drift.ts` beside `items.is_shelf_available` and `fees.outstanding_cents` — generated rather than computed in the service because it is the tiebreak the whole matrix ranks on, and two code paths computing it differently is the most damaging bug available here. And `circulation_rules_resolve_idx`, which §3 proposes as `(priority DESC, specificity DESC, id) WHERE enabled`, is NOT created: measured harmful, because at the 500-rule acceptance size on PG 16.15 the planner never chose it and forcing it read 403 buffers against 5 for the seq scan and sort, a whole-table read through a btree being random-order heap access. There is no `LIMIT 1` path for it to serve — `resolveCirculationPolicy` takes a whole `PolicySnapshot` and `resolve.ts` re-sorts in JS with `compareRank`, whose id tiebreak is UTF-16 code-unit order — so the SQL order reaches no answer and an `id` column here would only carry the ICU-el-GR-versus-code-unit divergence into a place nothing reads. The five policy foreign keys are `ON DELETE RESTRICT` so that deleting a named policy fails at the delete rather than as `POLICY_NOT_IN_SNAPSHOT` at one desk days later; `loans.applied_rule_id` deliberately has none, because a loan must keep pointing at the rule that priced it forever.

circulation_settings.reason: NOT A §3 TABLE, AND DELIBERATELY NOT `tenant_settings`. That one is named by §3's Platform line and stays `deferred / various` — "owned by the phase that first needs it" — because what phase 13 needs is ONE boolean, `circulation_rules_enabled`, not a cross-cutting settings singleton whose other columns belong to phases that have not been designed. Creating it here would mean inventing them, which is the guess this whole manifest exists to refuse, and it would hand every later phase a table it has to migrate rather than create. It also cannot be `public.tenant_settings`, the 1.0 table: phase 20 renames `public` to `v1_archive`, at which point a 2.0 service reading it is reading an archive. AND IT IS NOT A PLAN FEATURE. `EffectivePlanService.unlimitedPlan` rewrites every plan boolean to TRUE whenever `BILLING_ENABLED` is false, which is the configuration this product ships, so a plan-gated `circulation_rules_enabled` would be ON for every library — the exact inverse of §8 risk 6's "simple mode is the DEFAULT" — and `PlanGuard` answers 402 Payment Required, which a five-person school library that never asked for a rules matrix has not earned. If the matrix ever becomes sellable, the established two-layer shape is `tenant_settings.reservations_enabled` layered UNDER the plan capability: the plan key grants it and this column stays the switch.

circulation_statistics.reason: §3 writes it "`circulation_statistics` (partitioned)" and nothing else. A ROLLUP, not a per-act stream: `loan_events` is already the per-act record, and a counter bumped inside the checkout transaction would be a hot row in exactly the transaction this phase is accepted on (25-way concurrent checkout of the same item) as well as costing one of the twelve statements a checkin is allowed. Rebuilt hourly from `loan_events` by `circulation-statistics-rollup`, so it can be repaired; an in-transaction counter can only be believed. The counters are COLUMNS rather than rows keyed by an enum, forced from three directions: a partitioned table's unique index must contain every partitioning column (0A000), the rollup is an ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, and an enum-predicate arbiter raises 42P10 through Prisma. Partitioned monthly on `period_start` with no DEFAULT partition, like `audit_log`, and rolled forward by `partition-maintenance` — the job the baseline assigned to phase 16 by name. NOT `@replicated`: it is derived.

fixed_due_date_ranges.reason: §3 names it once and gives no DDL. All three of `from`, `to` and `due_date` are `date`: they are civil dates, true in every timezone, and the instant is composed at resolution time from the branch's zone and `due_time_of_day_min`. Overlaps within a set are refused by an `EXCLUDE USING gist` on a `daterange(from, to, '[]')` — THE ONE PLACE `btree_gist` earns the installation the baseline gave it, because two term ranges can overlap PARTIALLY (15 Sep–20 Jan against 10 Jan–15 Jun), which a unique index cannot see, and `computeDueDate` takes the FIRST covering range, so an overlap makes the due date depend on row order. A CHECK also refuses `due_date` before `from`, which is a loan that is overdue at checkout.

fixed_due_date_sets.reason: §3 names it once and gives no DDL. The term-end model, which in Greece is a public-library case and not only an academic one, because school libraries run mid-September to mid-June. The table is a name and its ranges: a `fixed` loan policy names one set with `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, and a checkout on a date no range covers is `POLICY_ERROR.noFixedDueDateRange` — a refusal, because the alternative is a term loan silently reverting to a rolling one and nobody noticing until the books do not come back.

floating_rules.group: Holdings and items (identity/description: Cataloguing; circulation state: Circulation)
floating_rules.reason: RE-PHASED BY PHASE 15, from 9c/15 to 23, having reached the phase that was supposed to create it. Phase 15 owns the SELECTOR and added it — `shelving_locations.floating_group`, a nullable group name because floating is almost never library-wide. It does not own the RULES. §6 phase 23 states the whole decision ("an item owned by A, checked out at B, returned at C either floats or generates a transit per `floating_rules`") and carries the four-branch fixture that is the only thing able to test a single row of it; the decision itself is taken at CHECKIN, which is phase 16. Inventing the columns here would mean inventing them with no caller, no fixture and no test — which is the failure `patrons` names in its own docblock, and a table created empty and wrong is worse than one honestly deferred.

hold_groups.reason: §6 phase 17 names "group holds" and says nothing else. A group is a CANCELLATION RULE and not a queue: each member sits in its own bib’s queue at its own position and is promoted independently, and the group only says what happens when one of them is FULFILLED — the siblings are cancelled with a reason naming the group, so a reader is not handed four printings of the same novel. That is why there is no `hold_groups.queue_position` and no group lock domain: a promotion still serialises on ONE bib, and the sibling cancellation is an ordinary targeted rebalance in each of the others.

hold_policies.reason: §3 names it once and gives no DDL. Phase 17 owns the queue, promotion, transit and the shelf; this table is the CONFIGURATION those behaviours read, and it lands four phases early because a `circulation_rules` row names a `hold_policy_id` and the resolver refuses a rule whose policy the snapshot does not hold. ONE `currency char(3)` for the table rather than one per amount, and that is correct rather than tolerated: `placement_fee_cents` and `not_picked_up_fee_cents` are added to ONE patron account, `@libriant/shared/money` refuses a currency mismatch on every operation, so a policy whose two fees are in different currencies is not a policy anybody can charge — one column makes it unrepresentable instead of unpayable, and a consortium billing in two currencies expresses it as two policies selected on `owning_branch_id`. `pickup_policy = 'explicitSet'` with an empty {@link HoldPolicyPickupBranch} set has NO SQL CHECK — it would have to count rows in another table — so the service refuses the combination and the snapshot loader treats it as a validation failure, because the silent reading of it is "no pickup branches", i.e. every hold uncollectable.

hold_policy_pickup_branches.reason: NOT A §3 TABLE: §3 names `hold_policies` and does not decompose it, so the branches an `explicitSet` policy allows collection at had nowhere to go. A CHILD TABLE rather than the `text[]` its two sibling vocabularies (`forgive_on`, `request_types`) get, and the difference is referential integrity — these are `branches.id` values, Postgres cannot foreign-key the elements of an array, and a deleted branch would leave a dangling id in every policy that named it, failing at the desk rather than at the delete. It carries a SURROGATE key rather than the composite `(hold_policy_id, branch_id)` its content suggests, because `change_events.entity_id` is one text column and `lbr2_write_change_event` takes one primary-key column name: a composite key cannot be replicated at all, and a device that rebuilt an `explicitSet` hold policy without its pickup branches would hold a policy under which no hold can be collected. The pair is still unique.

hold_ratio_alerts.reason: Re-phased by 17. It is a COLLECTION-DEVELOPMENT signal — "twelve readers per copy, buy more" — and not a circulation mechanism: nothing in the queue, the promotion, the shelf or the transit reads it, and building it here would mean inventing a threshold, an owner and a delivery channel with no acquisitions module able to act on any of them. §6 phase 87 is collection analytics, CREW/MUSTIE weeding and demand forecasting, which is where a holds-to-copies ratio is a number somebody can spend money on.

holdings_records.group: Holdings and items (identity/description: Cataloguing; circulation state: Circulation)
holdings_records.reason: Created because a specified table foreign-keys to it — `items.holdings_record_id text NOT NULL REFERENCES holdings_records(record_id)`, which is also why the primary key is `record_id` and not `id`. Phase 15 added `is_default`, which is what makes §3’s promised auto-creation of a default holdings record safe: it carries a partial unique on (bib_id, branch_id) WHERE is_default, strictly narrower than the unqualified unique phase 11 refused. The 852/853-855/863-868 compressed-holdings statement and the mandatory holdings 008 are still phase 84’s.

holds.reason: §3 names it in the Circulation line and gives it no DDL. Its ONE paragraph (MASTER-ARCHITECTURE.md:415) is the whole specification, so every column is a phase-17 decision. Three NULL tests spell "open" rather than a status enum, for the measurement 45-items.prisma records: a parameterised enum predicate seq-scans at 1470 buffers against 2, still seq-scans with enable_seqscan off, and `ON CONFLICT` cannot infer an enum-predicate arbiter through a parameterised cast at all. `queue_position` is non-NULL exactly while a hold is waiting (`holds_position_iff_waiting`) and at least 1 (`holds_position_is_one_based`) — and the second is the phase’s acceptance criterion made ENFORCEABLE rather than merely tested, because under it the 1.0 blanket `WHERE queue_position > 0` decrement does not produce a wrong number, it ABORTS with 23514 the first time a suspended hold at position 1 is skipped.

item_status_history.reason: §3 names it in the Holdings and items line and gives it no DDL. Phase 15, and half of its headline claim: "Every transition writes history." Append-only — no updated_at, no archived_at — and it records the branch move as well as the status move, because a float and a transit receipt change where a copy is without changing what it is.

item_status_reasons.group: Holdings and items (identity/description: Cataloguing; circulation state: Circulation)

Not a §3 table by name — §3 gives `items.status_reason_id` a column and no REFERENCES clause — and created anyway, because "every transition writes history" is unanswerable without a vocabulary for WHY. Deliberately not the same thing as `not_for_loan_code`/`damaged_code`/`lost_code`, which are condition flags read by the `is_shelf_available` generated column; those three vocabularies have no table anywhere in lbr2 and stay with phase 21, which already owns `override_reasons`.

Phase 15: "only one open transfer per item is possible", enforced by a partial unique on `WHERE received_at IS NULL AND cancelled_at IS NULL`. Open is the absence of both endings rather than a status enum, measured: the enum predicate seq-scans even with enable_seqscan off, and `ON CONFLICT` cannot infer an enum-predicate arbiter through Prisma's parameterised cast at all.

loan_events.reason: §3 names it in the Circulation line and gives it no DDL — the word `effective_at` appears exactly once in the whole plan of record, in the phase-16 line — so every column is a phase-16 decision. `occurred_at` keeps the meaning `change_events`, `audit_log` and `item_status_history` already give it (when Postgres learned) and `effective_at` is the new one (when it happened, at a desk, in the world); they differ for an offline replay and for a Saturday book drop, and `accrueOverdue` must be fed the second or a wand that syncs on Monday charges three days of fine on a Friday return. It carries NO patron_id: §3 nulls `loans.patron_id` on return, and an event log keeping its own copy would make that anonymisation cosmetic. NOT `@replicated` — `loans` already is, so a device gets the state it needs to lend, and replicating the event log would put a second divergent answer beside `change_events`.

loan_policies.reason: §3 names it once and gives no DDL; every column is a field of `LoanPolicy` in `packages/circ-policy/src/types.ts`, which phase 12 fixed against 630 vectors. What was actually decided here is ENCODING. A `Duration` is TWO columns — `<field>_value integer` plus `<field>_unit` — and not a Postgres `interval`, because `'3 weeks'::interval` normalises to `21 days`, so the unit is UNRECOVERABLE on read, and the value is frozen verbatim into `loans.policy_snapshot` and into `fixtures/resolution-vectors.json`, which `cargo test` reads as a cross-language contract: a policy that came back in different units would no longer describe the loan it priced. `timestamptz + interval` is also evaluated in the SESSION TimeZone, which is Europe/Athens on the production host and UTC in a report pod. Every pair carries a named `<table>_<field>_pair` CHECK, hand-written because Prisma cannot express it, and the failure it exists for is `period_value = 14` with `period_unit` NULL: `addDuration` ends `const step = period.unit === 'weeks' ? 7 : 1`, so a NULL unit is silently priced in DAYS. `renewals_allowed` NULL is UNLIMITED and 0 is none — the sentinel INVERTS against 1.0, where `maxRenewals = 0` meant no renewals and `fineCapCents = 0` meant uncapped, so every crossing of that boundary needs an explicit `x === 0 ? null : x` or "no cap" becomes a cap of zero and every fine becomes €0.00.

loans.reason: §3 or §2 gives it a full CREATE TABLE block.

lost_item_fee_policies.reason: §3 names it once and gives no DDL; the columns are `LostItemFeePolicy`'s. `fixed_amount_cents` is required when `charge_basis = 'fixedAmount'` and meaningless otherwise, and the CHECK in the migration says so — the alternative is a policy that charges NULL. The other half of that line is deliberately NOT a constraint: `replacementPrice` against an item with no price is `POLICY_ERROR.noReplacementPrice`, a resolver refusal at the moment of charging, because whether an item has a price is not a fact about the policy and a schema that tried to hold it would be constraining the wrong table. The refund columns are separate booleans for the replacement and the processing fee because libraries genuinely differ: the copy came back, so the replacement is refunded; the staff time spent chasing it was still spent.

marc_record_locks.reason: §3 named this table in one list and specified no column of it. Phase 10b designed it from the acceptance criterion and from measurement: `record_id` is the PRIMARY KEY because Postgres refuses a liveness index predicate (42P17), so uniqueness lives in the key and liveness in the acquire predicate; `session_id` is in the guard because without it 25 tabs belonging to the SAME cataloguer all won a live lock (measured 25 winners, 0 refused); and `displaced_holder_user_id`/`displaced_reason` exist because the upsert that acquires is also the one that displaces, and clause 5 needs `lock_expired` and `lock_taken_over` to be distinguishable. Recorded as `skeleton` rather than `specified`: the document specified nothing, so this is a designed table and a later phase adding a column to it is expected.

notice_policies.reason: §3 names it in both the Circulation and the Notices inventory lines and gives no DDL for either. §4.4 is what makes it two tables and not three: "Circulation owns `notice_policies`/`notice_triggers` configuration and template selection through the shared specificity resolver", while the notification engine owns channels, quiet hours, digests and the renderer. This is the circulation half, and it is nearly empty on purpose — a name and its bindings, because the bindings in `notice_policy_templates` are the entire content. It lands now for `hold_policies`' reason: `circulation_rules.notice_policy_id` is `NOT NULL` and the resolver raises `POLICY_NOT_IN_SNAPSHOT` for a rule whose policy is missing.

notice_policy_templates.reason: NOT A §3 TABLE, AND DELIBERATELY NOT CALLED `notice_templates`. That name is taken: this manifest reserves it for phase 22's RENDERABLE template — subject, body, channel, `dedupe_key` — and it stays `deferred / 9d/22` here, because creating this row-selector under that name would force phase 22 to rename or overload the table it already owns. What this is, is the SELECTOR: this trigger, for this branch and this category, fires that template. `template_id` therefore carries NO foreign key — `notice_templates` does not exist until phase 22 and the resolver never dereferences the id, which is opaque in `NoticeTemplateBinding` — and that is honest rather than lax: it is the column phase 22 will constrain. THE SELECTOR WEIGHTS INVERT HERE, and it is the domain rather than an inconsistency: §4.1 gives a template branch 2 and category 1, the reverse of a circulation rule's category 32 and branch 8. A loan period is a property of WHO IS BORROWING — a child gets three weeks, a member of staff a term — while a notice is a property of WHO IS SENDING it, since the branch's name, address, hours and voice are in the text, so a library that rewrote its overdue letter for one branch means THAT letter even for a category with its own.

overdue_fine_policies.reason: §3 names it once and gives no DDL; the columns are `OverdueFinePolicy`'s, field for field. `count_closed_days = false` is the expensive setting and the one Greek libraries want: the accrual walks the CALENDAR, so a fine does not grow over Δεκαπενταύγουστος — which is why `calendars.defined_from` matters as much as `defined_to`, because an undefined day inside an overdue span has to be a refusal rather than a guess. `amount_per_interval_cents` is multiplied by an integer interval count and never rounded: `@libriant/shared/money`'s `multiplyRounded` is half-to-even, which is right for allocation and wrong for a rate, where €0.025 becomes €0.02. `suspension` is one nested object in `types.ts` and three nullable columns here under an all-or-nothing CHECK, because a JSONB suspension policy inserts half-written and then suspends a patron for `undefined` days. `forgive_on` IS an enum array — at most four values, a closed vocabulary, no referential integrity to keep — which is exactly the test `hold_policy_pickup_branches` fails, since it points at `branches` and Postgres cannot foreign-key the elements of an array.

patron_addresses.reason: §3 names it in the record-side inventory line and gives no DDL. ROWS RATHER THAN 1.0'S FIVE INLINE COLUMNS, and the case that forces it is ordinary: a student has a term-time address and a home address, and the overdue notice has to reach the one they are at. 1.0 holds exactly one, so a library with a student population keeps the second in the free-text notes field, where nothing can post to it and no notice can find it. Exactly one address per patron may be primary and that is `patron_addresses_one_primary`, a partial unique on `WHERE is_primary` rather than a rule in the service, because the service is what forgets when a second write path arrives — an import, a merge, phase 32's self-service edit. `undeliverable_at` is the column with consequences: it feeds `PatronBlockCode.address_unconfirmed`, which is the block a library needs before it posts a fourth letter to a house nobody lives in, and it is a stamped instant rather than a boolean so "since when?" is answerable. `valid_from`/`valid_to` are `@db.Date` because a tenancy runs from a civil date in every zone.

patron_auth_providers.reason: Record side with phase 14; identity side with phase 32 (OPAC).

patron_blocks.reason: THE ONE TABLE IN THIS PHASE §3 WRITES SQL FOR, AND STILL NOT `specified`: what :423-426 gives is a `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX`, not a `CREATE TABLE`. Four columns are named by its predicate — `patron_id`, `code`, `auto_generated`, `cleared_at` — and the severity, the reason, the `observed` JSON and both actor columns are designed, so `invented` is the honest label and the one line the document does give is here character for character. It is the DATA-1 lesson applied to blocks: recalculation is an `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` so a sweep racing a desk transaction settles in Postgres instead of aborting the librarian's checkout. Measured, 25 concurrent recomputes against one patron while a desk transaction holds it, 20 iterations: advisory lock + `ON CONFLICT` gave desk 20/20 and sweeps 500/500 with zero duplicates; advisory lock + DELETE-then-INSERT gave sweeps 272/500 (228 × 23505); and `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` + DELETE-INSERT destroyed the desk — 0/20, ZERO loans written. That third row is the finding worth carrying forward: every genuine block INSERT runs the `patron_id` foreign-key check, which takes a `FOR KEY SHARE` tuple lock on the patron row, and that lock plus the desk's `FOR UPDATE` deadlock at `40P01`. An advisory lock does not participate in the FK row-lock graph at all, which is why `platform/locks.ts` is the mechanism; a row lock on `patrons`, if one is ever genuinely wanted, must be `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`. The `ON CONFLICT` clause repeats the predicate word for word because inference requires it to IMPLY the index predicate and reports every mistake as the same unhelpful `42P10` — `ON CONFLICT (patron_id, code)` alone is `42P10`, and naming it as a constraint is `42704`, since a partial unique INDEX is not a CONSTRAINT. Two semantics fall out of that predicate and both are deliberate: a CLEARED row does not conflict, so block history accumulates instead of being overwritten, and a MANUAL block coexists with an auto block on the same code, so a sweep structurally cannot clobber a librarian's own decision.

patron_cards.reason: §3 names it in the record-side inventory line and gives no DDL. A SATELLITE TABLE WHERE 1.0 HAS NO CONCEPT AT ALL, and the second row is the entire point: a library with a lost-card policy needs the old barcode to keep resolving — so the desk says "this card was reported lost on the 3rd" rather than "unknown barcode" — while the new one becomes live, and an inline column on `patrons` cannot hold two. Hence two indexes on `barcode_norm`: `patron_cards_barcode_unique_live` is partial on `retired_at IS NULL`, and `patron_cards_barcode_idx` is deliberately NOT partial, because it serves THE DESK SCAN — the one query in this phase that runs on every circulation transaction — and a retired barcode must still resolve. The predicate is on `retired_at` rather than on `status` for the reason `items.is_shelf_available` is a generated column: Prisma emits `status = CAST($1::text AS patron_card_status)` and `enum_in` is only STABLE, so the planner can never prove an enum-predicate partial index. `barcode_norm` is a STORED column rather than an expression index because the normalisation is `@libriant/shared/greek`'s fold, which Postgres cannot reproduce inside an index, and `patron_cards_retired_pair` refuses `status = 'lost'` with a NULL `retired_at`, which is a card the live unique index would still treat as active.

patron_categories.reason: MOVED FORWARD ACROSS A MILESTONE BOUNDARY. It was `9c/14/32` because §3 lists it under Patrons and its record side belongs there; it is created now because the rules matrix's highest-weighted selector is `patron_category_id` — 32 against the branch's 8 — and a rule naming a category that does not exist is a rule that silently NEVER MATCHES. That is the failure `resolve.ts` structurally cannot see, because a non-matching selector is indistinguishable from a deliberate one, and the symptom is a wrong loan period rather than an error. Creating it here also gives `patrons.patron_category_id` the foreign key `40-circulation.prisma` promised to 9c. A GENUINE SKELETON, and the record side stays with phases 14 and 32: OPAC self-registration rules, guardian requirements under the Greek digital-consent age of 15, and card expiry are the hardest part of the patron schema and would be invented here with the least information. What is present is what the matrix and `PatronCategoryLimit` cannot do without — code, name, `min_age_years` for `BLOCK_CODE.ageRestriction`, and `can_be_proxy`, which is the one switch a rule cannot express.

patron_category_limits.reason: §3 names it once, in the Circulation line rather than the Patrons one, and gives no DDL. KEYED ON `patron_category_id`, WITH NO `id` OF ITS OWN: `PatronCategoryLimit` in `types.ts` has no id field — the category IS the key — and keying on it makes one-limit-per-category structural rather than a unique index somebody can forget; `holdings_records` set the precedent with `record_id`. The distinction from `circulation_rules.max_loans_for_rule` is real and is the one librarians ask about: a RULE ceiling is "at most 3 DVDs", a CATEGORY ceiling is "at most 20 items of any kind", a child at the ceiling of one is not at the ceiling of the other, and `blocks.ts` evaluates them separately so the refusal at the desk can say which one it hit.

patron_identifiers.reason: §3 names it in the record-side inventory line and gives no DDL, and §5 gives no scheme list either, so `PatronIdentifierScheme` is designed — deliberately short, every value one a library can point at on a document. KEPT OUT OF `patrons` ON A DATA-PROTECTION ARGUMENT, not a normalisation one: an ΑΦΜ, an ΑΜΚΑ and a student number are three different disclosures with three different retention arguments, and a library that collects one has not thereby collected the others. As nullable columns they are three fields nobody can audit; as rows they are a list the subject-access bundle renders and an erase deletes, which is why ΑΜΚΑ — special-category-adjacent under Greek law — is a value here at all: so it can be FOUND, not so it can be collected casually. `value_norm` is what `patron_identifiers_one_per_scheme` makes unique per patron and scheme, because a person has one ΑΦΜ and two rows means one of them is wrong, which is a thing to discover before erase time rather than during it. `patron_identifiers_lookup_idx` on `(scheme, value_norm)` serves the other direction, finding the patron FROM the identifier, which is the academic self-service case where a student number is what the reader knows. `patron_identifiers_other_has_label` is a CHECK because without it `other` becomes the bucket everything falls into and nothing in it can be interpreted afterwards.

patron_identities.reason: Record side with phase 14; identity side with phase 32 (OPAC).

patron_merges.reason: §3 names it in the record-side inventory line and gives no DDL; §6 phase 14's acceptance criterion is about the OTHER half — "an old card barcode resolves through `merged_into_id` in one hop, never a chain". Both halves are needed and neither substitutes for the other: `patrons.merged_into_id` is what a card scan FOLLOWS, and this is what a librarian READS when they ask why. The 1.0 author dedup is the counter-example that settles it — it recorded its survivor only in `audit_log.afterJson`, with no column, so a stale author id resolves to nothing to this day. `carried` holds the counts (cards, identifiers, addresses, loans, fees) and `collided` holds what could NOT move because it would have violated a unique index — a duplicate card barcode, the same ΑΦΜ on both records — retired rather than dropped and named here, so a merge that silently lost something is visible without re-deriving it from the audit log. Both foreign keys are `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, and `patron_merges_one_per_loser` makes losing a merge a once-only event: a second row for the same loser means the merge ran twice or the record was un-merged and re-merged, and both are things somebody has to look at. REPLICATED EVEN THOUGH A DEVICE CANNOT MERGE, because a device that cached the loser has to learn it has been superseded — without the row, a card scanned offline resolves to a record the server folded away last Tuesday.

patron_messages.reason: §3 names it in the record-side inventory line and gives no DDL, and names `patron_notes` beside it in the same line without saying how the two differ. THE DIFFERENCE IS WHETHER IT INTERRUPTS: a message is pushed at whoever opens the record and is dismissed; a note is filed and read when somebody goes looking. One table for both gives a desk screen that either interrupts on everything or on nothing, and the library then stops reading it. `acknowledged_at` is stamped rather than the row deleted, because "was this person told?" is the question the message exists to answer, and `patron_messages_unacknowledged_idx` is partial on it, keyed `(patron_id, audience)` — the desk asks only for the staff ones. `audience = 'patron'` is storable now and rendered by phase 32, because a message a library writes today should not have to be re-typed when the OPAC ships. Replicated for the reason the block table is: the offline core has to show the librarian what is standing in front of them, and a message that only exists on the server is a message nobody reads on the day the link is down.

patron_notes.reason: §3 names it in the record-side inventory line and gives no DDL. The real decision is not this table's columns but what stays OUT of it: `patrons.staff_notes` SURVIVES BESIDE IT ON PURPOSE. A one-line "prefers large print" is not a dated, attributed note, and forcing every scrap through a form with an author and a timestamp is how a field stops being used and the information migrates into the name — which is the 1.0 shape phase 35's migration adapters have to defend against, quarantining a patron whose notes contain an ΑΦΜ-shaped string rather than importing it. So the inline field keeps the scraps and this table holds what a librarian meant to put on the record: attributed, dated, editable, and ARCHIVED rather than deleted, with `patron_notes_live_idx` partial on `archived_at IS NULL` so retiring a note costs nothing at the desk and loses nothing for the person who later asks what was written about them.

patron_number_counters.reason: §3 names it in the record-side inventory line and gives no DDL; §6 phase 14 supplies the only requirement — "number minting (`UPDATE … RETURNING`, never `max()+1`)" — and that prohibition has a measurement under it: `perf-04` recorded 1.0 pulling every member number for the year into Node and taking the max, 47 ms and ~190 MB of RSS churn per create on a 100,000-member tenant, which makes a roster import O(n²) and unfinishable. That is the first thing a new customer does. ONE ROW PER YEAR, KEYED ON THE YEAR ITSELF, no surrogate id and no branch column: a single-row counter CANNOT deadlock, because deadlock needs two lockables taken in two orders and there is one. Measured on this shape, 25 clients × 40 mints gave 1,000 distinct contiguous sequences, zero duplicates, zero deadlocks, zero rollbacks; minting inside the enrolment transaction is still correct and 23.7× slower (187 ms against 7.9 ms with a 5 ms body) because the row lock is then held for the whole transaction and every enrolment queues behind the slowest one; and minting under REPEATABLE READ fails 94.8% of the time with `40001`. Seeded LAZILY rather than by the migration, because the seed value is per-tenant data (`max(patron_number)` for the year) that a schema migration has no business computing. THE ONE TABLE HERE WHOSE NON-REPLICATION IS A SAFETY PROPERTY rather than an omission: it is a write-side singleton whose whole purpose is a row lock in ONE database, and a device that had it would mint locally — two branches enrolling offline then hand out the same number, printed on two cards.

patron_privacy_settings.reason: Record side with phase 14; identity side with phase 32 (OPAC).

patron_reading_history.reason: Re-phased by 17 out of the circulation band it was parked in. It is the OPAC opt-in — §6 phase 33: "reading history opt-in wired to the anonymisation path" — and the anonymisation path it wires to is phase 16’s, which is already live: `loans.patron_id` is nulled and `anonymised_at` stamped in the same transaction as the return, by default. A history table built before the opt-in that populates it would be an empty table whose only effect is to make that default look negotiable.

patron_registrations.reason: Record side with phase 14; identity side with phase 32 (OPAC).

patron_relationships.reason: §3 names it in the record-side inventory line and gives no DDL. DIRECTIONAL: the row reads `from` IS THE `kind` OF `to`, so a guardian row is parent → child. The symmetric alternative needs two rows kept in step and gives no answer at all to "who is the adult here?", which is the only question the guardian case asks. `can_borrow` is a SEPARATE column from the kind and defaults false, because a guardian relationship is not automatically a borrowing right, and conflating the two is how a library hands a fourteen-year-old's reserved book to an estranged parent. `confirmed_at` exists and PHASE 14 NEVER SETS IT: Greek L.4624/2019 art. 21 puts digital consent at 15 and phase 33 builds the double opt-in, so this phase stores the relationship and asserts nothing whatever about consent — a column phase 33 has somewhere to write is cheaper than a migration on a table that by then has guardian rows in it. `patron_relationships_one_live_per_kind` is unique on `(from, to, kind) WHERE ends_at IS NULL`, because two live `guardian` rows between the same two people that disagree about `can_borrow` is a question with two answers, and `patron_relationships_not_self` refuses the typo that makes somebody their own guardian.

patron_sessions.reason: Record side with phase 14; identity side with phase 32 (OPAC).

patrons.reason: NO LONGER A SKELETON, WHICH IS WHY THE BASIS CHANGED: the baseline created this table because `loans.patron_id text REFERENCES patrons(id)` forced its primary key, and its entry said the columns were deliberately incomplete. Phase 14 filled them in, so that sentence is now false. §3 names `patrons` in the record-side inventory line and mentions it nine times, every one about BEHAVIOUR — anonymisation on return, merge resolving in one hop, minting by `UPDATE … RETURNING` rather than `max()+1` — and none about a column, so every column here is designed. They are 1.0's `members`, which is not a shortcut: those are the fields this product already collects from Greek libraries, and a 2.0 patron holding different ones would make phase 19's copy-forward lossy for nothing. What is NEW is `merged_into_id`, `expires_at`, `erased_at` as a first-class column, and the address, the card and the identifiers moving OUT into satellite tables. TWO INDEXES ON `patron_number`, AND THEY CANNOT BE ONE: measured on 50,000 rows where the prefix selects 10%, a plain btree under `en_US.UTF-8`, `el_GR.UTF-8` and ICU el-GR seq-scans `LIKE 'M-2026-%'` at 319 buffers and STILL seq-scans with `enable_seqscan = off` — no index path exists, it is not a costing preference — while `text_pattern_ops` bitmap-scans at 21. The uniqueness index stays PARTIAL (`WHERE archived_at IS NULL`) so an archived card's number is re-issuable, and `patrons_number_pattern_idx` is deliberately NOT partial, because the counter seed must see archived numbers and a partial predicate is not implied by an unqualified query (Seq Scan, 337 buffers against 21). No third index for equality: `text_pattern_ops` carries `=(text,text)` at btree strategy 3, checked in `pg_amop`. And NOT `COLLATE "C"`, which is phase 13's precedent for `circulation_rules_listing_idx` and the obvious thing to copy — as the only index it makes `LIKE` work and `patron_number = $1` SEQ SCAN, because the equality takes its collation from the column. The one-hop merge invariant is a DEFERRABLE constraint trigger with two clauses plus sorted `patron:` locks, because measured over 60 concurrent pairs the trigger alone let 59 of 60 chains form — each transaction's deferred check passes on a snapshot that cannot see the other's uncommitted row — and trigger + sorted locks let 0 of 60. A chain is not a latency problem: the lookup is a fixed 12 buffers at any depth and returns the WRONG patron, and the desk then charges the loan to a record with no cards, no blocks and a balance nobody sees.

reading_history_policy.reason: §3 names it in the record-side inventory line, then spends a paragraph on its BEHAVIOUR without ever giving a column: mode defaults to `anonymised`, school libraries to `none`, "an IFLA/NISO professional obligation and a Greek DPA answer, and it is a DEFAULT rather than a setting someone forgot to turn on". That last clause is what the migration implements — the `id = 1` row is INSERTed by the migration itself, not by a seed script, because a default nobody has stored is not a default, and this has to hold for the tenants phase 19's PL/pgSQL copy-forward creates without the application ever running. A SINGLETON, like `circulation_settings`, and per-library rather than per-branch on purpose: a branch-scoped policy means a patron's reading history is anonymised or not depending on which desk they happened to walk up to. The `CHECK (id = 1)` is hand-written UNQUOTED because `check:schema-conventions` allows an INTEGER `id` only when it can find that clause, and Prisma always quotes. `retain_months` is refused unless `mode = 'kept'`, since a retention window on `anonymised` is a library believing it retains something it does not, and NULL means "until the patron asks", the only honest default for a setting whose whole point is that the patron chose it. NOT REPLICATED, and not for the counter's reason: §3 puts the null-and-stamp in the return transaction, phase 16 owns that transaction and it runs on the server, so a device would be carrying configuration it never reads. PHASE 14 STORES IT AND NOTHING READS IT YET — there is no return path until phase 16, and an anonymisation written here would have no caller.

work_clusters.reason: Created ONLY because §3 writes bib_records.work_cluster_id with a REFERENCES clause. An id and its timestamps, nothing else. Phase 40 owns clustering, and §5 already fixes the hard part of its design — cluster_key must carry an EXPRESSION key beneath the work key or the Greek original and the English translation of Zorba collapse into one cluster. Inventing that six phases early, with nothing to test it against, is the guess this program avoids. Every work_cluster_id is NULL until then and the FK is deliberately not created.
